 TEAM: Differences in Growth Patterns for Bloomsdale Spinach Plants 
When Receiving a Mix of Quick and Slow Release Fertilizers with 
Earth Soil and Lunar Regolith Combinations 
 
TEAM SPACE CADETS #17120 
 
BACKGROUND: 
Humanity’s return to the Moon marks the beginning of another new chapter in our efforts to extend our 
knowledge and reach in the cosmos. The advancements we have made in so many technologies and fields of 
human progress have been nothing short of amazing and profoundly influenced by the contributions of the 
many fields involved in space exploration. We must continue to nourish our curiosity and hopes of one day 
becoming an interplanetary species. The Artemis program represents the next step in that progression. 
As we aim to establish a more permanent presence on the Moon, we face new and difficult challenges. One of 
these challenges is our ability to wean-off of our over reliance on having so much shipped from the Earth to the 
Moon. One of the very foundations of the Plant the Moon Challenge is the need to make more efficient use of 
the Moon’s own resources (in situ), for among other things, food production, including planting and cultivation 
of nutritional resources to meet the demands of our communities on the Moon. It is here where Plant the Moon 
Challenge takes form. On earth, among the many things discovered about the Moon was the presence of lunar 
soil, more precisely, lunar regolith. Lunar regolith certainly provides benefits but, also serious challenges 
including for example, it’s lack of basic organic matter for planting, partly because the lunar surface receives 
much radiation and many important micronutrients needed are lacking in the regolith. Also, lunar soil (regolith) 
can prove to be toxic because of a high presence of aluminum, which lowers the uptake of nitrogen in plants. It 
is after all nitrogen which makes it possible for the creation of chlorophyll and the process of protein production 
(basic to all life) possible for a plant’s health. Overcoming these challenges will prove crucial for sustainable 
long-duration space missions and potential human settlements on the Moon. 
Given the above and knowing that science has shown us that caloric demands on astronauts can easily exceed 
some 3,000 calories per day given factors like weightlessness, the impact of space travel and lunar life on 
muscles tissue and bone health, and the immune system, Team Space Cadets decided to research and 
experiment with the role of fertilizers as factors that could contribute to a more robust production of a rich and 
highly nutritious food source in the way of spinach (specifically the Bloomsdale variety) because of its 
nutritional value (Proteins, Vit. C, Iron, B6, Magnesium, Calcium and Potassium. One of our primary 
considerations was the factor of the time it could take for fertilizers to assist spinach plant growth in the absence 
of organic materials in the regolith. Because our experiment is focused on fertilizer contribution to spinach plant 
growth and maturation, and the significant challenges facing us as we experiment with regolith and its own 
characteristics, we decided to use a combination of fast release fertilizer to fuel the spinach plants and a slower 
release fertilizer to extend the duration of the time that the fertilizers might act upon the spinach plant’s growth 
time and overall health during our 8 week growth period. So, we asked ourselves, Could the presence of a 
fertilizer with rapid and slow-release characteristics help make for a more robust spinach result? 
Blood meal is considered a good fertilizer and a valuable source of nitrogen for plants. It is a natural byproduct 
derived from the blood of animals, often from slaughterhouses. Blood meal is a rich source of nitrogen, 
containing around 12-13% nitrogen by weight. Also, Feather meal can be a good fertilizer for leafy greens as it 
is a good source of slow-release nitrogen. Feather meal is a byproduct made from poultry feathers, and it

2 
contains high levels of nitrogen, providing a slow and steady release of this essential nutrient to the plants. This 
slow-release nature makes it a good choice for leafy greens, which can benefit from a steady supply of nutrients 
over time. It can provide a more sustained source of nitrogen and other essential nutrients, promoting steady and 
consistent growth in leafy green plants. When considering the use of blood meal or feather meal as a fertilizer 
for leafy green growth in regolith, the choice largely depends on the specific characteristics of the regolith, the 
growth stage of the plants, and the desired release characteristics of the nutrients. 
HYPOTHESIS: 
Team Space Cadets learned that a quick release fertilizer works quickly into the actual plant’s system and that a 
slow-release fertilizer acted with the same goal but over a longer period of time. And so we thought, this might 
benefit the plants growing in the presence of regolith with earth soil so that the they could receive the needed 
nitrogen from the fertilizer over a longer period in the different mixes of soil to regolith experiment containers. 
After some research and consideration we decided on the following hypothesis: 
Adding a combined Earth Soil with Blood meal and Feather meal fertilizers will provide a richer and more 
robust and sustained uptake of nitrogen nutrients to the spinach plants resulting in a more abundant and 
nutritious spinach crop. 
EXPERIMENT DESIGN: 
The setup for the experiment was a closed space (room). There was a table, signage on the wall with references 
to the experiment and caution. There was a First Aid kit and fire extinguisher next to the whiteboard. There was 
also a worktable with necessary equipment (soil tester, soil thermometer, pH test kits a small whiteboard on the 
wall, a thermometer, barometer instrument on the wall next to the whiteboard. There were 2 grow lights (Sansi 
36W Full-Spectrum grow light) placed over the plant containers table. A table fan was also be placed at a 
distance to provide a gentle circulation of air. Other measuring equipment was included (scale, measuring cups 
and measuring spoons, gardening tools, ID sticks, nitrile gloves, masks, etc.) The team would meet once weekly 
to collect the data, take pictures, and discuss the process. Each member had a task(s) assigned and rotated 
different data collecting responsibilities. There was always a camera for still and video. For each meeting the 
team had a WhatsApp chat group and phone contact information. Data collection methods included clipboards 
with pages for recording measurements and the recording of data with the measured data information 
(empirical) information from the weekly observations. 
Weekly routine for data collection: 
1. General photos and video of the growing table 
2. Photos and video of readings from temperature, barometer, and water drainage from each pot prior to 
updated data collection measurement. 
3. Discussion: review (quantitative and qualitative notes documented) 
4. Data collection order: Number of leaves, size of plant, changes in soil characteristics, temperature of 
soil, pH, drainage, etc. 
5. Make sure all instruments are clean and put away for next data collection. 
6. Clean-up area 
 
PROCEDURES: 
The experiment and Procedures were as follows: 
1 Control group of 4 containers (cow pots small): C1(100% Earth Soil no fertilizer

3 
amendment), C2 (100% Earth Soil no fertilizer amendment), C3 (100% Regolith simulant no fertilizer 
amendment), C4 (100% Regolith simulant no fertilizer amendment). The control group would be observed 
over the grow period. This group received water and the full-spectrum light but with no earth soil mix or 
amendment. 
 
3 Experimental groups of 3 containers each: 
XA1, XA2, XA3 50% Reg-sim/50% Potting Soil fertilizer Mix 
XB1, XB2, XB3 65% Reg-sim/35% Potting Soil fertilizer Mix 
 XC1, XC2, XC3 80% Reg-sim/20% Potting Soil fertilizer Mix 
Each experimental group container included a mix of organic Blood Meal fast-release and Feather Meal slow-
release mix fertilizers of the same amount (22 mL). The three experimental groups were observed over the grow 
period and data collected on differences and changes in plant growth behavior. The plants received a spritzer of 
water on a need’s basis observed when the environmental temperature was particularly high. The spritzer of 
water was not measured as it was just a little spray to keep plant temps tolerable and seedlings moist. 
To get a better sense of the plant cell health we used an Apple MacBook Pro laptop with Amscope software and 
an AmScope - 40X-2500X LED Digital Binocular Compound Microscope with 3D Stage + 5MP USB Camera 
for photography of Plant leaf cell structure and activity as this image would give us an indication of the plant’s 
health (photosynthetic activity). 
INDEPENDENT VARIABLE(S): 
- 
Each Experimental Group (XA1-3, XB1-3, XC1-3) had different volumes of Earth Soil to Regolith 
Simulant (50/50, 65/35, 80/2 respectively. 
- 
The exposure to lighting (14 hrs/day) was adjusted weekly according to the manufacturers of the grow 
lights 36w Sansi Full Spectrum Growing Light. 
DEPENDENT VARIABLES: 
• overall color of plant (other visual characteristics of appearance) 
• pH 
• humidity %RH 
• drainage of water 
• temperature of environment 
• number of leaves 
• height of plant (cm) 
• length of stem (cm) 
 
CONTROLLED VARIABLES: 
• watering (distilled) 125mL/week 
• lighting duration (@ 14 hours/day) 
• growing medium (same seeds, same size containers) 
 
The differences in experimental group composition of earth soil to regolith would be observed. We wanted to 
see if the differences in the mixes (50/50 or 65/35, or 80/20) made a difference in the growth and if it may have 
been that the combined fertilizers (fast and slow release) might have contributed to the plant growth.

4 
RESULTS 
 
From here on out n/a means not available and ntr means nothing to report. One of our first lessons was to learn 
that our first evidence of a germinating seed of the spinach was called a “cotyledons.” Cotyledons are NOT the 
first “true” leaves of the plant. In the spinach they look like blades of grass (long and skinny). They are part of 
the embryo or seed and indicate that germination is moving along. Cotyledons help the germinating seed 
receive light to strengthen the germination process of photosynthesis as the germination process occurs. 
 
WEEK 1 
 
Observations: Team Space Cadets sees sprouts breaking out from seed. There is yet no indication of completed 
germination. A couple of the plant containers show first cotyledons developing. pH is steady. Temperatures are warm for 
this kind and variety (Bloomsdale Spinach) of crop. Also, the humidity is rather high. These factors can affect plant 
growth and development. 
 
WEEK 2 
 
Observations: Cotyledons present throughout the experimental groups and control. Control Group with 100% regolith 
simulant show stems with little to no color and struggling cotyledons. Other cotyledons show long or leggy stems. By the 
end of the week cotyledons dominate. We are concerned that the plants appear “leggy.” This means that the stems are 
growing, like reaching for light, but the first “true” leaves remain absent from the experiment though a couple of plants 
seem to show tiny “true” leaves beginning to grow.

5 
WEEK 3 
 
Observations: All containers are showing germinated plants, good color, and “true” leaves. This was a turning point in 
the growth process. The colors of the plants looked good and the health of the leaves and stems appeared satisfactory. 
However, we also noticed that while some plants had robust looking development, others seemed to indicate a growing 
tendency for “legginess” and that this was not completely dependent on the Regolith/sim to Earth Soil percentages in the 
experimental groups. We also noticed a little yellowing in some of the plants. Growth and development was definitely 
taking place. 
 
WEEK 4 
 
Observations: By the end of week four, we noticed crowding of the plants that we understood would affect future growth 
and development of the plants. We decided to thin-out the plant containers. We also noticed more “legginess” and some 
clear signs of bolting taking place in some plants. Also sometimes referred to as “going to seed,” bolting is when a plant, 
spinach being one the greens that can bolt, starts the reproduction process or producing flowers and seeds before the plant 
has matured or produced the edible green spinach leaves (in our case). It has moved on to the next stage (reproduction) 
and “bolted” in the plant’s life rather than first producing the food (spinach). Bolting usually is caused by changes in 
temperatures and stress of the plants, also climates where the plants are being grown. Also, lack of nutrients, light, 
watering can cause the stress behind bolting. We also observed some yellowing and weakening in the plants generally. 
Generally, we noticed many healthy leaves. Our concern was that the bolting would put an end to the growth and 
development process. Temperature and humidity remained a concern throughout the time.

6 
WEEK 5 
 
Observations: After thinning the containers, we studied the plants and the bolting taking place. The end of week five 
marked a dramatic change toward much more bolting and a loss of spinach development. The flowering and reproduction 
of seeds became the main characteristic observed in the plants. Spinach leaves appeared very thin given the variety 
planted (Bloomsdale). Many stems seemed to be self-uprooting and turning pinkish. The 100% Earth Soil containers had 
much less or no bolting, but the yellowing, skinny leaves and size of plants it became obvious to us that the plants were 
undergoing stress. The photos of the cell structure also seemed to indicate less clearly identifiable cell wall structure, and 
this can indicate worsening health of the leaves or plants. Also, the lack of good cell walls can mean that a plant is losing 
its form, affecting the leaves shape and health, including the movement of water to different parts of the plant. The 
presence of premature bolting, flowering and seed reproduction was seen very present. After thinning out the plants, we 
left the healthiest plants in their respective containers and so the number of containers went down to one XA, one XB 
representation one XC representation, and one for each Control representation C1 and C3. 
 
WEEK 6 
 
Observations: Our plant cell pics continued to show signs of great stress, cellular failure and generally, plants not being 
well. Controls also showed extensive deterioration of plant life.

7 
WEEK 7 
 
Observations: By the end of week seven, most plants had fallen and were dried and dying. The leaves were mostly 
yellow. The stems we fallen and had turned mainly pinkish or less green and more pinkish or clearer. It appeared as if the 
roots had gone bad or had been affected by different things that could have affected the plants (too much light, 
temperatures that were too much for the type of plant, a lack of organic nutrients, too much stress from excessive nitrogen 
presence, too little or too much water, etc). 
 
WEEK 8 
 
Observations: By the end of week eight (growing) nearly all the plants had died or were in that process. Only the 100% 
Earth Soil Control container showed some signs of plant life, though very little. All others appeared had died or were in 
that process with the roots pushing upwards. These plants also had fallen and dying stems. Generally, it seemed clear to 
the team that much research needed to be explored in the future for a better spinach planting, growing and harvesting 
future. 
 
Before continuing with the following analysis and conclusion statements, Team Space Cadets needs to address 
the makeup of the team. The team was originally composed of three members. Within three to four weeks the 
team lost two of its members. The principal investigator remained alone to complete his commitment to the 
PTMC and the experiment begun on the 5 of February. On the one hand, one of the team members was chosen 
to compete in London at an International Language Arts Olympics in Oxford and Cambridge Universities. The

8 
other team member, I must assume, lost interest. That said, I continued with the experiment, learned much, and 
am grateful for being able to complete this opportunity. My coach has shared much guidance and many 
resources from which I have learned and continue to learn. 
 
ANALYSIS CONCLUSIONS: 
When we decided on the plant to be chosen, we were interested, not in what might be easy to grow, but what might be 
most nourishing and what we could learn. And so we chose Spinach for reasons mentioned earlier, and particularly, the 
Bloomsdale variety. Our tropical environment here on the island (Puerto Rico) is quite capable of growing other variety 
types of spinach like Malabar, which is more resistant to heat, but not necessarily, as nutritious. We chose our set-up, 
design, and procedures to best fit a closed environment in a lunar community because outdoor growth on earth cannot be 
replicated on the moon, and so the need for a controlled growing environment as much as possible. 
 
We knew that Regolith/simulant lacks in basic organic materials and micronutrients for plants. We also wanted to have 
represented different Regolith to Earth Soil mixtures hoping for a better result in the 80/20 Reg/sim to Earth Soil (CX1-3) 
that the other two (AX1-3 50/50 and XB1-3 65/35). The key objective was to experiment with something that would 
actually reduce reliance and costs related to fuel and lunar missions. Our research was focused on plant growth and so we 
wanted to work with fertilizers. We also learned that there are fast-release and slow-release fertilizers and that given these 
options maybe the proper use of both would serve as a boost to the initial planting process and a slower release fertilizer 
would help the plants receiving the much-needed nitrogen over a longer period of time. The lack of organic material in the 
regolith/simulant would then receive the important nitrogen needed to produce the green in the spinach plants and help 
with leaf development and stem growth. The combination of the two sources of nitrogen might also help the plants with 
the production of K (Potassium) and P (Phosphorous). But we are also aware that too much nitrogen can be very toxic to 
plants also. So, we planted and observed. 
 
The first couple of weeks were productive and showed us that Cotyledons, in the case of many plants, have a very 
important role in the germination process. Plants began to grow, and leaves began to show indications of good growth and 
health. To us, the first two weeks were critical, and they were successful as first steps. This seemed to be shared by the 
three experimental groups. Weeks three and four had us excited about the growth and expectations. It did appear that the 
fertilizer mixes with the AX 50/50, BX 65/35, and even some of the CX 80/20 group were responding well. Yet, by the 
beginning of week 5 and throughout the rest of the growing period we began to see much legginess, yellowing, and 
bolting. This progressed throughout weeks 6-8 with weeks 7 and 8 showing lots of dead or dying plants. Team Space 
Cadets cannot say that the use of the fertilizer mixes was absolute in giving advantage to any of the three experimental 
groups though a slight advantage was recorded favoring groups XA (50/50) and XB (65-35). It seems, more specific and 
isolation of different variables might get us closer to that kind a a position. Also, factors like climate, temperatures and rH 
could have been detrimental to better growth. So was our hypothesis supported by the evidence? Yes, and no. Nothing 
definitive, as in without a doubt, was made so clearly by the end of the growth period. Part of the problem may well have 
been the amount of light or nitrogen in the experiment. Repeating what we said above nitrogen is very necessary but can 
also be very toxic, also humidity, temperatures, and other questions. In the future, we would like to dig deeper into the 
chemical composition of regolith and its possibilities of changing it when combined with organic materials. For example, 
instead of plants, maybe experiment and monitor different chemical components in different soils with the chemical 
materials in lunar regolith/simulant.
